content: Clindesse Vaginal Cream is indicated for the treatment of bacterial vaginosis in non-pregnant patients. It is administered as a single dose by inserting one full applicator intravaginally. Cleocin Vaginal Cream is also used for bacterial vaginosis and is administered intravaginally using one full applicator at bedtime for either 3 or 7 consecutive days in non-pregnant patients, and for 7 consecutive days in pregnant patients. Cleocin Vaginal Ovules are administered by inserting one suppository into the vagina at bedtime for 3 consecutive days. Xaciato is another treatment option, administered as a single dose of 100 mg clindamycin (in 5 g of gel) intravaginally. Bacterial vaginosis, previously referred to as Haemophilus vaginitis, Gardnerella vaginitis, nonspecific vaginitis, Corynebacterium vaginitis, or anaerobic vaginosis, is treated in females aged 12 years and older. The safety and efficacy of these treatments have not been established in females under 12 years of age. Adverse effects associated with clindamycin use include upper respiratory infections, pruritic rash, pruritus, erythema, diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, hypersensitivity reactions, and dizziness. Reproductive system-related side effects may include dysfunctional uterine bleeding, dysuria, dysmenorrhea, intermenstrual bleeding, menorrhagia, pelvic pain, vaginal burning, irritation, vulvar erythema, vulvitis, vulvovaginal discomfort or pain, dryness, and vulvovaginitis. Serious adverse effects include pseudomembranous colitis and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS). Clindamycin is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to clindamycin or other lincosamides, regional enteritis, ulcerative colitis, or a history of Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea. Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including clindamycin. The severity can range from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. If CDAD is suspected or confirmed, discontinuation of ongoing antibiotic use not directed against C. difficile may be necessary. Management includes fluid and electrolyte replacement, protein supplementation, and targeted antibiotic treatment for C. difficile. Barrier contraceptives, such as condoms or diaphragms, should not be used concurrently with or for 5 days following treatment with clindamycin vaginal creams or suppositories. These products contain mineral oil or oleaginous bases that may weaken latex or rubber products. Clindamycin vaginal products have been used in pregnant women during the second and third trimesters, but their safety in pregnancy has not been fully studied. It is unknown if clindamycin is excreted in human breast milk following vaginal administration, though it has been detected in breast milk after oral or intravenous administration. Clindamycin may affect the gastrointestinal flora of breastfed infants. Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibacterial agent that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible bacteria, interfering with peptide chain initiation. Clindamycin phosphate is inactive in vitro but is converted in vivo through hydrolysis to the active clindamycin compound. Vaginal administration at bedtime is recommended to reduce leakage. This information is provided for general educational purposes. For the most current and specific details, consult the applicable healthcare provider or plan provider.
